V7-001.topic: NAC in non-paracetamol ALF: Lee 2009 and Squires 2013
V7-001.q: What did the trials of N-acetylcysteine in non-paracetamol acute liver failure show, and which patients benefit?
a: **Lee 2009** (Gastroenterology, US ALF Study Group): double-blind RCT, **173** adults with non-paracetamol ALF, IV NAC for 72 h (81) vs placebo (92).
Primary outcome, overall 3-week survival: **70% vs 66%**, not significant. NAC does not improve overall survival.
Transplant-free survival: **40% vs 27%** (one-sided p = 0.043). Transplant rate 32% vs 45% (not significant).
By coma grade: **I–II: 52% vs 30%** (p = 0.010); **III–IV: 9% vs 22%**, no benefit. The gain is confined to early encephalopathy.

**Squires 2013** (Hepatology, paediatric ALF group): **184** children with non-paracetamol ALF. 1-year survival 73% vs 82% (not significant); 1-year transplant-free survival **lower with NAC: 35% vs 53%** (p = 0.03).
Under 2 years with grade 0–1 HE: transplant-free survival 25% vs 60%. NAC is not used routinely in paediatric non-paracetamol ALF.
Bedside: adult, non-paracetamol, grade I–II HE: start IV NAC early (ACG 2023 suggests it). Grade III–IV: it does not replace listing. Any chance of paracetamol: give NAC.
V7-001.src: Lee WM et al., Gastroenterology 2009;137:856; Squires RH et al., Hepatology 2013;57:1542; ACG Clinical Guideline: Acute Liver Failure (Shingina A et al., Am J Gastroenterol 2023)

V7-002.topic: SNAP 12-hour acetylcysteine regimen and the two-bag regimen
V7-002.q: What is the SNAP regimen for paracetamol poisoning, and what is the evidence for it?
a: Why change: the 21-hour regimen gives 150 mg/kg in the first hour. That early peak drives **anaphylactoid** reactions and vomiting, and three bags are complex to run.
**SNAP** (Scottish and Newcastle Antiemetic Pre-treatment): **100 mg/kg over 2 h**, then **200 mg/kg over 10 h**. Same total **300 mg/kg**, in **12 hours**.
**Bateman, Lancet 2014**: RCT, **222** patients, 2×2 design with ondansetron. Vomiting, retching or rescue antiemetic at 2 h: **39/108 vs 71/109** (adjusted OR **0.26**).
Severe anaphylactoid reactions: **5 vs 31** patients (adjusted OR **0.23**). ALT rise above 50%: 13/112 vs 9/110, no significant difference; not powered for non-inferiority.
Ondansetron pre-treatment cut vomiting (OR 0.41) but was linked to more ALT rises (16 vs 6 patients), so it is not routine.

Status: **RCEM 2023** recommends SNAP as the default in UK emergency departments for adults and children. Australia and New Zealand (2019) use a **two-bag** regimen: **200 mg/kg over 4 h**, then **100 mg/kg over 16 h**.
Stopping rules do not change: stop when paracetamol is undetectable, ALT is falling and INR is under 2; otherwise continue at the last-bag rate (APAP-10).
V7-002.src: Bateman DN et al., Lancet 2014;383:697 (SNAP); RCEM position statement on the SNAP regimen, 2023; Chiew AL et al., Med J Aust 2020;212:175 (ANZ paracetamol guideline)

V7-003.topic: Plasma exchange in ALF: Larsen 2016, volume and who
V7-003.q: What is the evidence for plasma exchange in acute liver failure, what volume is used, and in which patients?
a: **Larsen, J Hepatol 2016**: open multicentre RCT, **182** ALF patients: standard medical therapy (90) vs standard therapy plus **high-volume plasma exchange** (92) for **3 days**.
Volume: **15% of ideal body weight** (about **8–12 L**) exchanged against fresh frozen plasma each day, for 3 days.
Result: hospital survival **58.7% vs 47.8%** (HR **0.56**, 95% CI 0.36–0.86, stratified for transplant). The primary end-point was transplant-free survival.
Why it works: attenuated innate immune activation and multi-organ dysfunction; SIRS and SOFA scores fell more with exchange (p < 0.001).
No gain when given only as a bridge in patients who went on to transplant (p = 0.75).
Who (EASL 2017): plasma exchange improves transplant-free survival; the benefit is greatest when it is started **early** and in patients who **will not be transplanted**.

Standard volume (1.5–2 plasma volumes): **Maiwall 2022** RCT, 40 patients, 21-day transplant-free survival **75% vs 45%** (HR 0.30); less SIRS and lower ammonia and SOFA by day 5: an option where grafts are scarce.
V7-003.src: Larsen FS et al., J Hepatol 2016;64:69; EASL Clinical Practical Guidelines on acute (fulminant) liver failure, J Hepatol 2017;66:1047; Maiwall R et al., Clin Gastroenterol Hepatol 2022;20:e831

V7-004.topic: Acute fatty liver of pregnancy: Swansea criteria and treatment
V7-004.q: What are the Swansea criteria for acute fatty liver of pregnancy, and how are AFLP and HELLP treated?
a: **Swansea criteria** (Ch'ng, Gut 2002): AFLP is diagnosed with **6 or more of 14** features when no other cause explains them.
Clinical: vomiting, abdominal pain, polydipsia or polyuria, encephalopathy.

Laboratory: bilirubin **>14 µmol/L**, glucose **<4 mmol/L**, urate **>340 µmol/L**, white cells **>11 × 10⁹/L**, AST or ALT **>42 IU/L**, ammonia **>47 µmol/L**, creatinine **>150 µmol/L**, PT **>14 s** or APTT **>34 s**.
Imaging and tissue: ascites or bright liver on ultrasound; **microvesicular steatosis** on biopsy (rarely done because of bleeding risk).
Why it helps: HELLP shares the raised enzymes and low platelets; hypoglycaemia, ammonia, coagulopathy and polyuria are liver FAILURE features that point to AFLP.
AFLP treatment: ICU, **IV glucose**, correct DIC with FFP and cryoprecipitate, then **deliver once stabilised**; liver transplant is rarely needed.
HELLP treatment: magnesium, blood pressure control and **delivery**; steroids for fetal lungs if preterm. Both usually improve after delivery.
V7-004.src: Ch'ng CL et al., Gut 2002;51:876 (Swansea criteria; cut-offs as tabulated in later reviews)

V7-005.q: What is the October 2026 global multi-society definition of acute-on-chronic liver failure, and how is it graded?
a: **October 2026**: AASLD with **EASL, APASL**, ALEH (Latin America) and SOLDA (Africa) published one consensus definition of ACLF (81 statements), jointly in Hepatology, J Hepatol, Ann Hepatol and Hepatol Int.

Substrate: **advanced chronic liver disease** (fibrosis F3 or more, or cirrhosis). Core requirement: **liver failure**, bilirubin **≥5 mg/dL** and INR **≥1.5**, plus at least one extrahepatic organ dysfunction or failure.
**Type A**: arises in compensated advanced CLD or cirrhosis. **Type B**: arises in previously decompensated cirrhosis.

Organ failures: kidney = **KDIGO AKI stage 2–3** or new RRT; brain = **West Haven grade 3–4** HE or ventilation for HE; circulation = vasopressor need (not HRS-AKI alone); lung = ventilation, P/F **≤225** or S/F **≤244**.
Grades: **1** = liver failure plus one extrahepatic organ dysfunction (e.g. KDIGO stage 1 AKI); **2** = plus one organ failure; **3** = plus **two or more** organ failures.
Bedside: it builds on the APASL Kyoto consensus (2025) and the 2025 organ-failure definitions; regional definitions are not withdrawn, so I still name EASL-CLIF grade and APASL criteria.
V7-005.src: Bajaj JS, Lucey MR et al., Acute-on-Chronic Liver Failure: A Global Multi-Society Consensus on Definitions, Hepatology 2026 (doi 10.1097/HEP.0000000000001891); AASLD press release 30 Oct 2026; HCPLive summary 30 Oct 2026

V7-006.q: Spotter: the Glasgow-Blatchford score. What goes into it, and how do you use it?
a: Pre-endoscopy score from bedside data only; range **0–23**. It predicts the need for intervention (transfusion, endoscopic therapy, surgery) or death.
Others: pulse 100 or more = 1; **melaena** = 1; **syncope** = 2; **hepatic disease** = 2; **cardiac failure** = 2.
Use: **GBS ≤1** = very low risk of rebleeding or death; ESGE 2021 allows outpatient care without early endoscopy (Blatchford's original cut-off was 0).
Why urea scores high: blood digested in the upper gut is absorbed as protein, so a raised urea points to an upper source.
Catch: it is a triage score. Almost every ICU bleeder scores high, so in the ICU it decides little; the full Rockall needs endoscopic findings.
V7-006.src: Blatchford O et al., Lancet 2000;356:1318; Gralnek IM et al., Endoscopy 2021;53:300 (ESGE NVUGIH update)

V7-007.topic: Upper GI bleed evidence: Villanueva 2013, HALT-IT 2020, ESGE 2021
V7-007.q: What is the evidence for the transfusion threshold and against tranexamic acid in upper GI bleeding, and what goes before the scope?
a: **Villanueva** (NEJM 2013): **921** patients, single centre. Restrictive: transfuse at Hb **<7**, target 7–9. Liberal: at <9, target 9–11. Exsanguinating bleeds, ACS and stroke were excluded.
Result: 6-week survival **95% vs 91%** (HR 0.55); further bleeding **10% vs 16%**; adverse events 40% vs 48%.
Cirrhosis: benefit in Child-Pugh **A/B** (deaths 4% vs 12%), none in Child C. Liberal blood raised the HVPG (20.5 to 21.4 mmHg): more volume, more portal pressure, more rebleeding.
ESGE 2021: threshold **≤7 g/dL**, target 7–9. With cardiovascular disease: threshold **≤8**, target **≥10**.

**HALT-IT** (Lancet 2020): **12,009** patients; TXA 1 g, then 3 g over 24 h, vs placebo. Death from bleeding at 5 days **4% vs 4%** (RR 0.99); venous thrombosis **0.8% vs 0.4%** (RR 1.85). So: no TXA.
Before the scope (ESGE 2021): high-dose IV PPI may be considered but must not delay endoscopy; IV erythromycin if bleeding is severe or ongoing.
Timing: endoscopy within **24 h** after resuscitation; urgent (≤12 h) gives no better outcome in non-variceal bleeding. Suspected varices: within **12 h** (Baveno VIII 2026).
V7-007.src: Villanueva C et al., NEJM 2013;368:11; HALT-IT Trial Collaborators, Lancet 2020;395:1927; Gralnek IM et al., Endoscopy 2021;53:300 (ESGE); Baveno VIII Faculty (Berzigotti A et al.), J Hepatol 2026, doi:10.1016/j.jhep.2026.07.030 (Baveno VIII)

V7-008.topic: HRS-AKI trials: CONFIRM and ATTIRE; terlipressin cautions
V7-008.q: What did CONFIRM and ATTIRE show, and what are the side effects of terlipressin?
a: **CONFIRM** (Wong, NEJM 2021): **300** patients with HRS type 1 (199 terlipressin, 101 placebo), albumin in both arms. Terlipressin 1 mg 6-hourly, 2 mg from day 4 if creatinine fell under 30%, up to 14 days.
Verified HRS reversal **32% vs 17%** (p = 0.006). 90-day mortality **51% vs 45%**: no survival benefit.
Harm: respiratory failure **14% vs 5%**; deaths from respiratory disorders by day 90 **11% vs 2%**. Likely mechanism: albumin volume load plus a raised afterload.
FDA boxed warning: do not start if **SpO2 <90%**, stop if it falls below 90%; higher risk with volume overload; avoid in **ACLF grade 3**; creatinine **>5 mg/dL** unlikely to benefit.
Other side effects: myocardial, mesenteric and digital **ischaemia**. Boluses give more blood-pressure swings and respiratory failure than an infusion.
**ATTIRE** (China, NEJM 2021): **777** patients with decompensated cirrhosis and albumin <30 g/L. Daily 20% albumin targeted to **≥30 g/L** for up to 14 days vs standard care.
Composite of infection, kidney dysfunction or death (days 3–15): **29.7% vs 30.2%**, no benefit. More pulmonary oedema or fluid overload (23 vs 8 serious events).
So: albumin for defined indications (SBP, large-volume paracentesis, HRS-AKI), not to correct a number; adjust it daily to volume status and stop it if overloaded (ADQI/ICA 2024).
V7-008.src: Wong F et al., NEJM 2021;384:818 (CONFIRM); China L et al., NEJM 2021;384:808 (ATTIRE); TERLIVAZ prescribing information (FDA 2022); Nadim MK et al., J Hepatol 2024;81:163 (ADQI/ICA)

V7-009.topic: Stress ulcer prophylaxis: SUP-ICU, PEPTIC and the trade-off
V7-009.q: Besides REVISE, what do the trials show on stress ulcer prophylaxis, and what is the pneumonia and C. difficile trade-off?
a: **SUP-ICU** (Krag, NEJM 2018): **3,298** acutely ill ICU adults at risk of bleeding; pantoprazole 40 mg IV daily vs placebo.
90-day mortality **31.1% vs 30.4%** (RR 1.02): no difference. Clinically important GI bleeding **2.5% vs 4.2%**. Infectious events (pneumonia, C. difficile) **16.8% vs 16.9%**.
**PEPTIC** (JAMA 2020): cluster crossover, 50 ICUs, **26,982** patients; PPI vs H2 blocker as the unit default. In-hospital mortality **18.3% vs 17.5%** (RR 1.05, 95% CI 1.00–1.10): not significant.
PEPTIC bleeding **1.3% vs 1.8%** (RR 0.73) in favour of PPI; C. difficile not different.
REVISE (NEJM 2024) adds, in ventilated patients: bleeding **1.0% vs 3.5%** (NNT 40), VAP 23.2% vs 23.8%, C. difficile 1.2% vs 0.7% (not significant).

The trade-off: acid suppression lets bacteria grow in the stomach, the feared route to pneumonia, C. difficile and SBP. Large blinded trials have not shown that harm; the bleeding benefit is real but small.

Catch: in SUP-ICU's sickest third (**SAPS II >53**) mortality trended higher with pantoprazole (RR 1.13, 95% CI 0.99–1.30; interaction p = 0.05); SCCM/ASHP 2024 call the PPI mortality effect in high-severity patients uncertain.

So (**SCCM/ASHP 2024**): low-dose PPI or H2 blocker only with **coagulopathy, shock or chronic liver disease** (ventilation alone is not a firm risk factor; REVISE came later); stop when the risk resolves and before ICU discharge.
V7-009.src: Krag M et al., NEJM 2018;379:2199 (SUP-ICU); PEPTIC Investigators (Young PJ et al.), JAMA 2020;323:616; Cook D et al., NEJM 2024;391:9 (REVISE); MacLaren R et al., Crit Care Med 2024;52:e421 (SCCM/ASHP)

V7-010.topic: Modified Marshall organ failure; no single best severity score
V7-010.q: How is organ failure defined in acute pancreatitis, and which severity score is best?
a: Revised Atlanta defines severity by **organ failure**, not by a score: **persistent >48 h = severe**, transient (<48 h) = moderately severe.
Organ failure = **modified Marshall score ≥2** in any of three systems:

**SYSTEM** | **SCORE 2 MEANS**
**Respiratory** | PaO2/FiO2 **201–300** (or lower)
**Renal** | Creatinine **170–310 µmol/L (1.9–3.6 mg/dL)** (or higher)
**Cardiovascular** | SBP **<90 mmHg, not fluid-responsive** (off inotropes)
**No single best score.** ACG 2024: scoring systems and imaging alone predict severe disease poorly (good negative, poor positive predictive value).
What helps at the bedside: **SIRS**, **rising BUN**, **haematocrit >44%**, obesity and comorbidity on admission; reassess over the first **48 h**.
Persistent SIRS or organ failure despite fluids → monitored bed or ICU. Persistence, not the admission number, defines severe disease.
V7-010.src: Banks PA et al., Gut 2013;62:102 (revised Atlanta 2012); Tenner S et al., Am J Gastroenterol 2024;119:419 (ACG 2024 guideline)

V7-011.topic: CT spotter: chronic calcific pancreatitis vs pancreatic necrosis
V7-011.q: Spotter: CT abdomen of the pancreas. Is this chronic calcific pancreatitis or necrosis, and what are the local complications?
a: **Chronic calcific pancreatitis:** coarse **calcifications** (mostly intraductal stones), focal or diffuse; CT is the most sensitive test for them.
Main duct **dilated and beaded** (chain of lakes: strictures and dilatations); dilated if over about 5 mm in the head; parenchymal **atrophy**; pseudocysts are common.
Cause: mostly **alcohol**. **Tropical calcific pancreatitis** (India): young, non-alcoholic, large dense stones in a markedly dilated duct; SPINK1 link.
**Necrosis (acute):** on contrast CT, **non-enhancing pancreatic parenchyma**, with or without peripancreatic necrosis. Early perfusion can look patchy; trust it after the first week.
**Gas** in a pancreatic or peripancreatic collection = presumed **infected necrosis**.

**COLLECTION** | **UNDER 4 WEEKS (NO WALL)** | **OVER 4 WEEKS (WALLED)**
**Fluid only** | APFC | **Pseudocyst**
**Fluid + necrosis** | ANC | **WON**
V7-011.src: Banks PA et al., Gut 2013;62:102 (revised Atlanta 2012: collections, necrosis on CECT); Garg PK, Narayana D, Glob Health Epidemiol Genom 2016;1:e17 (tropical calcific pancreatitis, SPINK1); Learning Radiology and Articl.net radiology notes on chronic pancreatitis CT

V7-012.topic: Infected necrosis trials: PANTER, TENSION, POINTER
V7-012.q: What did PANTER, TENSION and POINTER show about infected necrotising pancreatitis?
a: **PANTER** (van Santvoort, NEJM 2010; 88 pts): step-up (drain, then VARD) vs open necrosectomy. Major complications or death **40% vs 69%** (RR 0.57); mortality 19% vs 16% (NS).
PANTER: new multiple organ failure **12% vs 40%**, incisional hernia 7% vs 24%, new diabetes 16% vs 38%. **35%** of step-up patients needed percutaneous drainage only.
**TENSION** (van Brunschot, Lancet 2018; 98 pts): endoscopic vs surgical step-up. Major complications or death **43% vs 45%** (NS); mortality 18% vs 13% (NS).
TENSION: endoscopic had fewer pancreatic fistulas (**5% vs 32%**) and shorter stay (53 vs 69 days).
**POINTER** (Boxhoorn, NEJM 2021; 104 pts): drainage within 24 h of diagnosis vs postponed until walled off. Comprehensive Complication Index **57 vs 58** (NS); mortality 13% vs 10%.
POINTER: postponed arm had fewer interventions (**2.6 vs 4.4**) and fewer necrosectomies (22% vs 51%); **39%** never needed drainage (antibiotics and support alone).
Bottom line: antibiotics first, **wait for walling-off (~4 weeks)**, then step-up, endoscopic where feasible.
V7-012.src: van Santvoort HC et al., N Engl J Med 2010;362:1491 (PANTER); van Brunschot S et al., Lancet 2018;391:51 (TENSION); Boxhoorn L et al., N Engl J Med 2021;385:1372 (POINTER)

V7-013.topic: Calorie targets, the trials and indirect calorimetry
V7-013.q: What calorie target do you set in early critical illness, what is the evidence, and how does indirect calorimetry change it?
a: **ESPEN 2023**: hypocaloric, **≤70%** of energy expenditure in the early phase; after **day 3**, increase to **80–100%** of measured expenditure. **ASPEN 2022**: **12–25 kcal/kg/day** for the first 7–10 days.
**Indirect calorimetry**: ESPEN recommends it in ventilated patients. Without it, ventilator-derived VCO2 (or PA-catheter VO2) is preferred to predictive equations.
Why not 100% of the measured value early: calorimetry measures total expenditure, part of which is met by endogenous glucose; feeding it all on top **overfeeds**.
**PermiT** (Arabi, NEJM 2015, n=894): 40–60% vs 70–100% of calories, same protein: 90-day mortality **27.2 vs 28.9%**, not significant.
**TARGET** (NEJM 2018, n≈4000): 1.5 vs 1.0 kcal/mL enteral, similar protein in both (about 1863 vs 1262 kcal/day): 90-day mortality **26.8 vs 25.7%** (RR 1.05, 0.94–1.16).

**EAT-ICU** (Allingstrup, ICM 2017, n=199): calorimetry-guided full target plus protein ≥1.5 g/kg from day 1: no better 6-month physical function (SF-36 PCS 22.9 vs 23.0), more hyperglycaemia and insulin.
**NUTRIREA-3** (shock): 6 vs 25 kcal/kg for 7 days: low was ready for ICU discharge sooner. Lesson: calorimetry sets the target, not the speed.
V7-013.src: Singer P et al., Clin Nutr 2023;42:1671 (ESPEN ICU); Compher C et al., JPEN 2022;46:12 (ASPEN/SCCM); Arabi YM et al., NEJM 2015;372:2398 (PermiT); TARGET Investigators, NEJM 2018;379:1823 (TARGET); Allingstrup MJ et al., Intensive Care Med 2017;43:1637 (EAT-ICU); Reignier J et al., Lancet Respir Med 2023;11:602 (NUTRIREA-3)

V7-014.topic: Protein dose: EFFORT Protein and PRECISe
V7-014.q: What protein dose do you give in the ICU, and which patients were harmed by high protein?
a: **ESPEN 2023**: up to **1.3 g/kg/day** delivered **progressively**. **ASPEN 2022** made no new recommendation and kept **1.2–2.0 g/kg/day**.
**EFFORT Protein** (Heyland, Lancet 2023, n=1329, 85 ICUs): ventilated, high nutritional risk; prescribed **≥2.2 vs ≤1.2** g/kg/day, delivered **1.6 vs 0.9**.
Result: discharge alive by day 60 **46.1 vs 50.2%** (RR 0.91, 0.77–1.07); 60-day mortality **34.6 vs 32.1%** (RR 1.08), no benefit.
Harmed: baseline **AKI** (time to discharge alive HR 0.5; 60-day mortality RR 1.4, mainly those **not on RRT**) and **SOFA ≥9** (HR 0.8). Exploratory subgroups; urea rose with high protein.
**PRECISe** (Bels, Lancet 2024, n=935, double-blind): enteral **2.0 vs 1.3** g/kg/day: worse EQ-5D-5L health utility to 180 days (mean difference −0.05, −0.10 to −0.01); mortality HR 1.14 (NS).
PRECISe also: more GI intolerance with high protein (OR 1.76). Two RCTs, no benefit from more than about 1.3 g/kg early.
What I do: build to about 1.2–1.3 g/kg/day; avoid early high doses in AKI not on RRT and in high SOFA; on CRRT give more to replace losses.
V7-014.src: Singer P et al., Clin Nutr 2023;42:1671 (ESPEN ICU); Compher C et al., JPEN 2022;46:12 (ASPEN/SCCM); Heyland DK et al., Lancet 2023;401:568 (EFFORT Protein); Stoppe C et al., Crit Care 2023;27:399 (EFFORT AKI analysis); Bels JLM et al., Lancet 2024;404:659 (PRECISe)

V7-015.topic: Feeding in shock: NUTRIREA-3, trophic vs full
V7-015.q: Should you feed a ventilated patient in shock, and how much in the first week?
a: **NUTRIREA-3** (Reignier, Lancet Respir Med 2023, n=3044, 61 French ICUs): ventilated adults on vasopressors, early feeding for the first 7 days.
Arms: low **6 kcal/kg/day** + protein **0.2–0.4 g/kg/day** vs standard **25 kcal/kg/day** + **1.0–1.3 g/kg/day**.
Result: ready for ICU discharge sooner with low (median **8 vs 9 days**, HR 1.12, 1.02–1.22); 90-day mortality **41.3 vs 42.8%** (NS).
Low also had less vomiting (HR 0.77), diarrhoea (0.83), **bowel ischaemia (0.50)** and liver dysfunction (0.92); secondary infections no different.
**NUTRIREA-2** (n=2410, shock): full-dose EN vs PN: bowel ischaemia **2% vs <1%** (HR 3.84) and more colonic pseudo-obstruction, no survival gain.
Why: in shock the splanchnic bed vasoconstricts; digestion raises gut oxygen demand, so full feeds risk non-occlusive bowel ischaemia.
What I do: no EN in uncontrolled shock; once stable on steady or falling vasopressors, low-dose EN; stop for distension, rising lactate or IAP; advance after shock resolves.
V7-015.src: Reignier J et al., Lancet Respir Med 2023;11:602 (NUTRIREA-3); Reignier J et al., Lancet 2018;391:133 (NUTRIREA-2); Singer P et al., Clin Nutr 2023;42:1671 (ESPEN ICU)

V7-016.topic: EN vs PN trials: CALORIES, NUTRIREA-2, EPaNIC
V7-016.q: What is the trial evidence for enteral versus parenteral nutrition, and when does parenteral nutrition become necessary?
a: **CALORIES** (Harvey, NEJM 2014, n=2400, 33 UK ICUs): early PN vs EN within 36 h for 5 days: 30-day mortality **33.1 vs 34.2%**; no more infections with PN; EN had more vomiting and hypoglycaemia.
CALORIES: both arms fell short of the 25 kcal/kg target, so it compared routes at similar, low intake.
**NUTRIREA-2** (Reignier, Lancet 2018, n=2410, ventilated in shock): EN vs PN: 28-day mortality **37 vs 35%**, ICU infections 14 vs 16% (NS); EN had more vomiting, diarrhoea, bowel ischaemia.

**EPaNIC** (Casaer, NEJM 2011, n=4640): late PN (day 8) vs early PN to top up EN: ICU infections **22.8 vs 26.2%**, 6.3% more likely to leave ICU alive earlier (HR 1.06), less cholestasis, RRT 3 days shorter.
EPaNIC: ICU, hospital and 90-day mortality the same (90-day 11.2% in both). Early supplemental PN adds harm without survival gain.
**PEPaNIC** (Fivez, NEJM 2016, n=1440 children, 3 PICUs): withholding PN to day 8: new infections **10.7 vs 18.5%**, PICU stay 2.7 days shorter; 90-day mortality 5.3 vs 6.8% (NS).
**When PN**: ESPEN 2023: if EN is contraindicated, PN within **3–7 days**; early progressive PN in severe malnutrition; supplemental PN case by case in week 1.
**ASPEN 2022**: EN or PN acceptable in the first week; do not start supplemental PN before **day 7**.
V7-016.src: Harvey SE et al., NEJM 2014;371:1673 (CALORIES); Reignier J et al., Lancet 2018;391:133 (NUTRIREA-2); Casaer MP et al., NEJM 2011;365:506 (EPaNIC); Fivez T et al., NEJM 2016;374:1111 (PEPaNIC); Singer P et al., Clin Nutr 2023;42:1671 (ESPEN ICU); Compher C et al., JPEN 2022;46:12 (ASPEN/SCCM)

V7-017.topic: Gastric residual volume: NUTRIREA-1 and REGANE
V7-017.q: Do you measure gastric residual volume, and what is the evidence against routine GRV?
a: GRV was used to predict aspiration, but checking it mainly interrupts feeds and reduces delivered calories.
**NUTRIREA-1** (Reignier, JAMA 2013, n=449 ventilated, early EN): no GRV monitoring vs GRV every 6 h: VAP **16.7 vs 15.8%** (difference 0.9%, 90% CI −4.8 to 6.7; margin **10%**), non-inferior.
NUTRIREA-1: more vomiting without GRV monitoring, but more patients reached their calorie target.
**REGANE** (Montejo, Intensive Care Med 2010, n=329): GRV limit **500 vs 200 mL**: more diet delivered in week 1 (**88.2 vs 84.5%**); pneumonia, ventilation time and ICU stay similar.
**ESPEN 2023**: delay EN if GRV **>500 mL/6 h**; give a prokinetic, **IV erythromycin** first line for 24–48 h; if large GRV persists, post-pyloric feeding rather than stopping EN.
ESPEN adds: continued GRV measurement during established EN may not be necessary.
What I do: no routine GRV; look for vomiting, distension and rising IAP; exclude obstruction or ischaemia before pushing feed.
V7-017.src: Reignier J et al., JAMA 2013;309:249 (NUTRIREA-1); Montejo JC et al., Intensive Care Med 2010;36:1386 (REGANE); Singer P et al., Clin Nutr 2023;42:1671 (ESPEN ICU)

V7-018.topic: NUTRIC score: what it predicts and how it changes feeding
V7-018.q: What does the NUTRIC score predict, how does it change feeding, and how strong is the evidence?
a: **NUTRIC** (Heyland, Crit Care 2011): age, APACHE II, SOFA, comorbidities, days in hospital before ICU, IL-6. **Modified NUTRIC** drops IL-6 (high risk **≥5** of 9).
Validation (Rahman, Clin Nutr 2016; RCT database, n=1199): each point raised the odds of 28-day death about **1.4-fold**.
Key claim: higher nutritional adequacy went with better survival in **high** scorers but not in low scorers (interaction p=0.029). This is **observational**, post hoc.
How it changes feeding: high score, start EN early and reach target without delay; if EN is impossible in a malnourished patient, early progressive PN rather than none (ESPEN).
Low score: less urgency; supplemental PN can wait until after the first week.
**ASPEN/SCCM 2016**: high nutrition risk = **NRS 2002 ≥5** or **NUTRIC ≥5** (without IL-6), or severe malnutrition: advance EN toward goal over **24–48 h**, watching for refeeding (expert consensus).
Caution: RCTs did not confirm that high-risk patients gain from more feeding: **EFFORT Protein** (high nutritional risk) showed no benefit from higher protein.
**ESPEN 2023**: no nutrition score is validated for ICU; consider every patient staying **>48 h** at risk of malnutrition. The score is mostly illness severity.

V7-019.topic: Liver complications of PN (IFALD): spectrum and prevention
V7-019.q: What are the hepatic complications of parenteral nutrition, and how do you prevent them?
a: **IFALD** (intestinal failure-associated liver disease, formerly PNALD): liver injury linked to intestinal failure and PN, without another primary liver disease, hepatotoxin or biliary obstruction.

Spectrum: **steatosis** (early), **cholestasis** (raised ALP, GGT, conjugated bilirubin), gallbladder **sludge and stones**, then **fibrosis**. Steatosis and cholestasis can reverse; fibrosis much less.
Causes: excess **dextrose and energy** (hepatic fat); **soybean lipid** (omega-6, plant sterols, low α-tocopherol) impairs bile flow; **sepsis**; long PN; no enteral feed, so biliary stasis.
ICU evidence: in **EPaNIC**, delaying PN to day 8 lowered the incidence of **cholestasis** and **gallbladder sludge**, although plasma bilirubin was slightly higher.
Prevent: avoid overfeeding; pure soybean lipid **<1 g/kg/day**, use composite fish-oil-containing emulsions if more is needed; lipid infusion ≤**0.11 g/kg/h**.
Also: **cycle PN**, keep some oral or enteral intake, treat sepsis promptly, avoid hepatotoxic drugs.
If it develops: exclude obstruction and drugs (ultrasound), cut dextrose and soybean lipid, switch to a fish-oil-containing emulsion, advance enteral feed.

V7-020.topic: Glutamine in burns: RE-ENERGIZE and REDOXS
V7-020.q: What is the role of glutamine in burns, and why is it not routinely recommended?
a: Rationale: glutamine is **conditionally essential** in catabolism, a fuel for enterocytes and immune cells; levels fall after major burns. Small early trials suggested fewer infections.
**RE-ENERGIZE** (Heyland, NEJM 2022, n=1200, deep burns ≥20% TBSA at 18–39 y, lower thresholds if older): enteral **0.5 g/kg/day** vs placebo until 7 days after the last graft.
RE-ENERGIZE result: time to discharge alive **40 vs 38 days** (HR 0.91, 0.80–1.04); 6-month mortality **17.2 vs 16.2%**; no difference in serious adverse events.

**REDOXS** (Heyland, NEJM 2013, n=1223, ventilated, ≥2 organ failures): IV **0.35 g/kg/day** + enteral 30 g/day: 28-day mortality **32.4 vs 27.3%** (OR 1.28, p=0.05, borderline); 6-month **43.7 vs 37.2%** (HR 1.18, significant).
REDOXS: harm was greatest with baseline **renal dysfunction** (post hoc); urea rose with glutamine.

**MetaPlus** (van Zanten, JAMA 2014, n=301): high-protein feed enriched with glutamine, omega-3 and antioxidants vs high-protein: new infections **53 vs 52%**; 6-month mortality in medical patients **54 vs 35%**.

**ESPEN 2023**: still lists enteral 0.3–0.5 g/kg/day for 10–15 days in burns >20% (Grade B), but notes the largest RCT was negative and says it needs revision; no glutamine for other ICU patients; no IV glutamine if unstable or in liver or renal failure.
What I do: no routine glutamine in burns; early EN, protein 1.5–2 g/kg/day, micronutrients, avoid overfeeding.

questions.text: Acute liver failure — ICU management.

steps.bridge: ALF is INR 1.5 or more with encephalopathy, no prior liver disease, under 26 weeks. Next: the cause decides the first drug →
Each cause has its own treatment: NAC, aciclovir, antivirals, delivery. Next: the brain-protecting ICU bundle →
NAC, sodium 145–155, early CRRT for ammonia, and no FFP for a number. Next: circulation, kidney, bleeding and glucose →
Target CPP, continuous RRT, correct clotting only for bleeding, watch glucose. Next: the second killer, infection →
Infection is common and silent, so culture daily; prophylaxis does not save lives. Next: who needs a new liver →
King's criteria pick those who will die without a graft. Next: graft type, and when it is too late →

spine: What it is: **INR ≥1.5** plus encephalopathy within **26 weeks**, no prior liver disease. I manage it in ICU and call the transplant centre on day one.
Cause first: NAC for paracetamol (and early-grade non-paracetamol), aciclovir for HSV, **entecavir or tenofovir** for hepatitis B, delivery for AFLP or HELLP.
Brain: intubate grade III–IV, head up 30°, sodium **145–155** with hypertonic saline, early CRRT if ammonia is above **150 µmol/L**; avoid fever and hypercapnia.
Systems: **noradrenaline**, then vasopressin, to CPP above **60**; continuous RRT; daily cultures; dextrose for low glucose; FFP only for bleeding or a procedure (INR is prognostic).
Listing: King's (paracetamol pH **<7.30**, or INR >6.5 + creatinine >3.4 + grade III–IV; non-paracetamol INR >6.5 or 3 of 5), Clichy, or ALFED 4 or more.
Caution: King's is specific but misses up to a third who die, so I reassess daily. Too late: fixed pupils, ICP above 50 with CPP below 40, uncontrolled sepsis.

questions.text: What are the King's College criteria?

steps.bridge: Paracetamol side rests on acidosis or the triad; non-paracetamol side on INR or 3 of 5. Next: the faster lactate add-on →
Modified King's adds lactate, which flags death hours earlier. Next: how well the paracetamol criteria perform →
Specific about 90% but sensitive only about 60%: not meeting them does not reassure. Next: the alternatives, Clichy and the rest →
Clichy uses factor V with deep HE; phosphate and lactate refine paracetamol cases. Next: the Indian dynamic score →

spine: What it is: **O'Grady 1989** (588 patients, King's College Hospital): criteria that predict death without transplant in ALF. Meeting them means list.
Paracetamol: arterial **pH <7.30** after fluids, or all three of **INR >6.5**, creatinine **>3.4 mg/dL** and grade III–IV encephalopathy.
Non-paracetamol: **INR >6.5**, or any 3 of: age <10 or >40, non-A non-B or drug cause, jaundice to HE >7 days, INR >3.5, bilirubin >17.5 mg/dL.
Modified: lactate **>3.5** early or **>3.0** after fluids (Bernal 2002) raised sensitivity from 76% to 91% and flagged deaths sooner (median 4 vs 10 h).
Caution: specific (about 90%) but poorly sensitive (about 60%). In India I add Clichy (factor V) and ALFED, which is dynamic over 3 days.

questions.text: What is the role of N-acetylcysteine in non-paracetamol acute liver failure?

steps.bridge: Beyond paracetamol NAC acts as an antioxidant and vasodilator; the trial used a 72-hour IV regimen. Next: what the trials showed →
No overall survival gain; transplant-free survival rises only in coma I–II adults, never in children. Next: grading that coma →
Grade I–II is confused or drowsy; III–IV no longer responds to voice. Next: NAC in the ICU bundle →

spine: Mechanism: beyond paracetamol, NAC is an **antioxidant** that replenishes glutathione, vasodilates and improves microcirculation and oxygen delivery.
Evidence: **Lee 2009**, 173 adults: overall 3-week survival **70% vs 66%**, not significant; transplant-free survival **40% vs 27%**.
Who benefits: coma grade **I–II**, transplant-free survival **52% vs 30%**; grade III–IV **9% vs 22%**, no benefit.
Children: **Squires 2013**, 184 children: no survival gain and lower 1-year transplant-free survival (**35% vs 53%**), worst under 2 years.
What I do: IV NAC early in adult non-paracetamol ALF with grade I–II HE, as ACG 2023 suggests. It never delays listing, and I do not use it routinely in children.

questions.text: NAC protocol for paracetamol poisoning.

steps.bridge: The nomogram from 4 hours decides who needs NAC; staggered doses bypass it. Next: how NAC protects, and when →
NAC refills glutathione; protection is near complete within 8 hours. Next: the classic 21-hour regimen →
Three bags, 150 + 50 + 100 = 300 mg/kg in 21 h; the fast first bag causes reactions. Next: the 12-hour SNAP fix →
Same 300 mg/kg in 12 h with far fewer reactions and less vomiting. Next: when to stop or continue →

spine: Why NAC: it replenishes glutathione to detoxify **NAPQI**. Within **8 hours** protection is near complete, and it still helps later.
21-hour IV: **150 mg/kg over 1 h**, **50 mg/kg over 4 h**, **100 mg/kg over 16 h** (300 mg/kg). Oral: 140 mg/kg, then 70 mg/kg 4-hourly for 17 doses.
SNAP: **100 mg/kg over 2 h**, then **200 mg/kg over 10 h**: the same 300 mg/kg in **12 hours**.
Evidence: **Bateman, Lancet 2014**, 222 patients: vomiting OR **0.26**, severe anaphylactoid reactions **5 vs 31**, no difference in ALT rise.
What I do: SNAP is the RCEM default in the UK; Australia uses two bags (200 mg/kg over 4 h, 100 over 16 h). Stop when undetectable, ALT falling, INR <2.
Caution: anaphylactoid reactions are rate-related, not IgE: pause, antihistamine, restart. SNAP was not powered for non-inferiority on liver injury.

questions.text: Hepatic encephalopathy management.

steps.bridge: Ammonia becomes glutamine in astrocytes: slow in cirrhosis, abrupt oedema in ALF. Next: what tips a cirrhotic into HE →
Bleeds, infection, low potassium, sedatives and constipation raise brain ammonia. Next: the six-step treatment →
Airway, precipitant, lactulose to 2–3 stools, rifaximin, normal protein. Next: why ALF is a different disease →
In ALF the swelling is cytotoxic plus vasogenic, so cerebral oedema kills. Next: ammonia as the number to act on →
High arterial ammonia predicts oedema and death; lactulose and LOLA fail, CRRT works. Next: the general ICP measures →
Head up, neck neutral, avoid hypercapnia, hyponatraemia and fever. Next: the osmotic tools and the sodium target →
Hypertonic saline to sodium 145–155, mannitol for surges. Next: the whole ALF bundle on one card →

spine: Cirrhosis: find and treat the precipitant, protect the airway in grade 3–4, **lactulose** to 2–3 soft stools, add **rifaximin 550 mg** twice daily, no protein restriction.
Mechanism: ammonia becomes glutamine in astrocytes. Slow in cirrhosis, so little oedema; abrupt in ALF, so **cerebral oedema** and intracranial hypertension.
ALF difference: arterial ammonia above **150 µmol/L** marks high risk. Lactulose and rifaximin are not recommended, and LOLA does not lower ammonia.
What I do: intubate grade III–IV, head up 30°, hypertonic saline to **Na 145–155**, early **CRRT** for ammonia (ACG 2023: grade 2 HE or more), mannitol for surges.
Evidence: CRRT cut ammonia 38% over 3 days and was linked to lower 21-day transplant-free mortality (OR **0.47**; Cardoso 2018).
Caution: in ALF, deepening HE is a transplant trigger, so I list early; I also avoid hypoglycaemia, fever and sedative excess.

questions.text: What is the role of plasma exchange in acute liver failure?

steps.bridge: No bioartificial or albumin-dialysis device has shown a survival benefit. Next: the one therapy that did →
High-volume exchange, 15% of ideal body weight for 3 days, raised hospital survival. Next: standard volume and mechanism →
Standard-volume exchange also helped (75% vs 45%), a cheaper option. Next: Indian results by cause →

spine: What it is: exchanging the patient's plasma for FFP removes circulating toxins and inflammatory mediators and replaces clotting factors.
Evidence: **Larsen 2016**, 182 patients: hospital survival **58.7% vs 47.8%** (HR **0.56**), with falls in SIRS and SOFA scores.
Volume: high volume is **15% of ideal body weight** (8–12 L) a day for **3 days**; standard is 1.5–2 plasma volumes (Maiwall 2022: TFS **75% vs 45%**).
Who: EASL 2017: greatest benefit when started **early** and in those who will **not be transplanted**; no gain as a bridge in those who got a graft.
What I do: start it early in high-risk ALF, especially when no graft is available or the patient is not a candidate, alongside CRRT.
Caution: large FFP volumes, and it corrects the INR, so the INR no longer tracks prognosis. In ACLF it is used only in trials (EASL 2023).

questions.text: ACLF — how do you differentiate it from ALF and decompensated cirrhosis?

steps.bridge: ALF needs a previously healthy liver, INR 1.5 or more and HE within 26 weeks. Next: what changes when the liver was already sick →
ACLF is chronic disease plus a trigger plus organ failure, with high early mortality. Next: three definitions disagree on who counts →
APASL takes hepatic triggers in CLD without prior decompensation; EASL-CLIF any trigger in cirrhosis. Next: the APASL sequence →
APASL: bilirubin 5 or more and INR 1.5 or more, then ascites or HE within 4 weeks. Next: how EASL-CLIF grades it →
Grade 1 is kidney failure alone; grades 2 and 3 are two and three or more failures. Next: what each grade means for survival →
Mortality climbs steeply with grade, about 22%, 32% and 77% at 28 days. Next: the 2026 global multi-society definition →

spine: ALF: no prior liver disease, **INR ≥1.5** with encephalopathy within **26 weeks**. Decompensated cirrhosis: ascites, HE, bleed or jaundice, without organ failure.
ACLF: acute deterioration of chronic liver disease with **organ failure** and high short-term mortality; systemic inflammation is the hallmark.
EASL-CLIF (CANONIC): cirrhosis, any trigger. Grade 1: kidney failure alone, or one other failure with kidney or brain dysfunction; grade 2: two failures; grade 3: three or more.
APASL 2019: jaundice (bilirubin **≥5 mg/dL**) and coagulopathy (INR **≥1.5**), then ascites and/or HE within **4 weeks**, in CLD without prior decompensation.
Which I use: EASL-CLIF in the ICU (futility: CLIF-C ACLF above **70** at day 3–7); APASL for Indian HBV and alcohol flares; the **Oct 2026** global definition as common language.
Why it matters: 28-day mortality about **22%, 32% and 77%** for grades 1–3 (CANONIC); grade 1 may reverse, grades 2–3 need transplant evaluation.

questions.text: HELLP and acute fatty liver of pregnancy — how do you differentiate?

steps.bridge: HELLP is haemolysis, AST above 70 and platelets under 100,000 on a pre-eclampsia background. Next: the liver that truly fails →
AFLP is microvesicular fat with high INR and ammonia and low glucose. Next: the two side by side →
Low glucose, high ammonia and coagulopathy beyond the platelet count point to AFLP. Next: the Swansea criteria and treatment →
Six of 14 Swansea features make AFLP; both are treated by delivery after stabilising. Next: when to deliver in HELLP →
HELLP gets steroids and delivery after 48 h, or at once if the mother is unstable. Next: the exam summary →

spine: HELLP: haemolysis (LDH twice normal, schistocytes), AST above 70 and platelets **under 100,000**, usually with hypertension: a severe form of pre-eclampsia.
AFLP: third-trimester **microvesicular** fat with true liver failure: **hypoglycaemia**, high ammonia, coagulopathy, encephalopathy, often polyuria.
Telling them apart: platelets fall early in HELLP; glucose, INR and ammonia go wrong in AFLP. **Swansea criteria**: 6 or more of 14 features, no other cause.
Treatment: stabilise and **deliver**. HELLP: magnesium, BP control, steroids for fetal lungs if preterm. AFLP: IV glucose, FFP and cryoprecipitate for DIC.
Caution: the two overlap, so I treat the worst features. Liver failure that persists after delivery needs a liver unit; transplant is rarely needed.

questions.text: How do you manage upper GI bleed in the ICU?

steps.bridge: Even in cirrhosis only half of upper bleeds are varices; ulcers are the rest. Next: how to grade the risk before the scope →
The Glasgow-Blatchford score triages from bedside data; ≤1 is very low risk. Next: the trial evidence on blood, TXA and timing →
Transfuse at Hb 7, give no TXA, scope within 24 h. Next: the same rules applied to a cirrhotic case on warfarin →

spine: What it is: haematemesis or melaena from above the ligament of Treitz. In cirrhosis half are varices, but a quarter are still gastric ulcers.
Triage: Glasgow-Blatchford from urea, Hb, systolic BP, pulse, melaena, syncope, liver and heart failure. **GBS ≤1** is very low risk; ICU patients score high.
What I do: airway, two large cannulas, transfuse at Hb **<7**, target 7–9 (≤8 with heart disease). IV PPI; if varices are likely, terlipressin and ceftriaxone too.
Evidence: Villanueva 2013, **921** patients: restrictive transfusion gave 6-week survival **95% vs 91%** and less rebleeding; liberal blood raised portal pressure.
Endoscopy within **24 h** after resuscitation, **12 h** if variceal. Erythromycin before the scope if bleeding is active. No routine FFP for the INR in cirrhosis.
Caution: no tranexamic acid. HALT-IT, **12,009** patients: bleeding deaths 4% vs 4%, venous thrombosis almost doubled (**0.8% vs 0.4%**).

questions.text: How do you manage acute variceal bleeding?

steps.bridge: Varices bleed once the HVPG reaches 12; 20 or more predicts failure. Next: why portal pressure rises in the first place →
Portal pressure is resistance times splanchnic flow. Next: which drugs act on which half →
Vasoconstrictors cut inflow now; beta-blockers are for later; TXA has no place. Next: the full acute management →
Drug before the scope, antibiotic, banding, then tamponade or TIPS. Next: the doses and time limits of the bundle →
Terlipressin 2–5 days, ceftriaxone up to 7, Hb 7, band within 12 h. Next: who gets a TIPS early, and what a TIPS costs →
Pre-emptive TIPS within 72 h for Child C 10–13 or B >7 with active bleeding. Next: the bridge when bleeding cannot be stopped →

spine: What it is: bleeding from portosystemic collaterals once the HVPG is **≥12 mmHg**. An HVPG of 20 or more predicts treatment failure and death.
Mechanism: portal pressure = resistance × flow. Vasoactive drugs cut splanchnic inflow now; non-selective beta-blockers belong to the chronic phase.
What I do: terlipressin or octreotide before endoscopy for 2–5 days, ceftriaxone **1 g/day**, transfuse at Hb 7 to a target of **7–8**, no FFP, no TXA (Baveno VIII 2026).
Band within **12 h**. Pre-emptive TIPS within **72 h** (ideally <24 h): Child C 10–13, B >7 bleeding at scope, or HVPG ≥20. García-Pagán 2010: 1-year survival **86% vs 61%**.
If uncontrolled: rescue TIPS, bridged by a covered oesophageal stent (now preferred) or balloon tamponade after intubation, gastric balloon first, for no more than 24 h.
Caution: antibiotics are a survival treatment, not an option; over-transfusion raises portal pressure and rebleeding.

questions.text: How do you diagnose and treat spontaneous bacterial peritonitis?

steps.bridge: SBP is translocated gut bacteria in poorly opsonic ascites, deadly untreated. Next: how it presents and whom to tap →
Peritoneal signs are rare, so tap every admitted cirrhotic with ascites; INR is no bar. Next: how the fluid count decides →
Neutrophils of 250 or more mean treat, whatever the culture. Next: the organisms, and how to spot secondary peritonitis →
SBP is monomicrobial Gram-negative; polymicrobial with Runyon criteria means CT. Next: which antibiotic and for how long →
Third-generation cephalosporin 5 days, carbapenem if nosocomial, re-tap at 48 h if no better. Next: the albumin dose and why →
Albumin 1.5 g/kg then 1 g/kg on day 3 cut renal failure and death (Sort 1999). Next: the same decisions in a bedside case →
Treat on the count now, and give albumin to the high-risk. Next: preventing the next episode →

spine: What it is: infection of ascitic fluid without a surgical source, from gut bacterial translocation; mostly Gram-negative and monomicrobial.
Diagnosis: tap every admitted cirrhotic with ascites; the INR is no bar. Ascitic neutrophils **≥250/mm³** means treat now, whatever the culture.
Treatment: cefotaxime or ceftriaxone for 5 days, a carbapenem if nosocomial. Re-tap at 48 h if not improving; polymicrobial growth means secondary peritonitis.
Albumin: **1.5 g/kg** within 6 h of diagnosis, then **1 g/kg on day 3**. Why: it stops the inflammation-driven fall in effective volume that triggers hepatorenal syndrome.
Evidence: Sort 1999, **126** patients: renal impairment **10% vs 33%**, in-hospital deaths **10% vs 29%**. Benefit was greatest with bilirubin ≥4 or creatinine ≥1 mg/dL.
After: norfloxacin secondary prophylaxis, since recurrence is 60–70% a year without it, and referral for transplant.

questions.text: Hepatorenal syndrome — diagnosis and treatment.

steps.bridge: HRS is only a fifth of kidney injury in cirrhosis and is functional. Next: why the kidney clamps down →
Splanchnic vasodilatation and inflammation both end in renal vasoconstriction. Next: the formal ICA criteria →
HRS-AKI needs ascites, AKI, no volume response, no shock or structural injury; 2024 shortened it to 24 h. Next: the new names →
HRS-AKI replaced type 1; AKD and CKD replaced type 2. Next: how to give terlipressin and when to stop →
Terlipressin with albumin, infusion safer than bolus, up to 14 days; stop for ischaemia or hypoxia. Next: the ICU view →
Noradrenaline is the ICU alternative; response is creatinine within 0.3 of baseline. Next: the trials behind it →

spine: What it is: functional kidney failure in cirrhosis with ascites: splanchnic vasodilatation, low effective volume, renal vasoconstriction. About 20% of AKI in cirrhosis.
Diagnosis (ICA, revised 2024): AKI by creatinine or urine output, no response to volume within **24 h**, no shock, no nephrotoxins. Tubular injury or CKD no longer excludes it.
Treatment: stop diuretics and nephrotoxins; terlipressin, by infusion or 1 mg 6-hourly, with albumin 20–40 g/day. Noradrenaline is the ICU alternative. Transplant cures.
Evidence: CONFIRM, **300** patients: HRS reversal **32% vs 17%**, but no survival benefit (90-day deaths 51% vs 45%).
Side effects: respiratory failure **14% vs 5%**, respiratory deaths **11% vs 2%**; cardiac, gut and digital ischaemia. Do not start if SpO2 **<90%** or volume overloaded.
Albumin is not a number to chase: ATTIRE, targeting **≥30 g/L** in decompensated cirrhosis, gave no benefit and more pulmonary oedema.

questions.text: Who needs stress ulcer prophylaxis?

steps.bridge: Prophylaxis only while risk factors persist, by any route, never past ICU discharge. Next: the largest blinded trial →
REVISE: pantoprazole cut bleeding 1.0% vs 3.5%, no change in death or VAP. Next: the earlier trials and the infection trade-off →
SUP-ICU and PEPTIC showed less bleeding, no mortality effect, no clear infection harm. Next: where the sepsis guideline lands →

spine: What it is: prophylaxis against stress-related mucosal bleeding. Clinically important bleeding is now uncommon: **3.5%** in ventilated patients on placebo in REVISE.
Who (SCCM/ASHP 2024): **coagulopathy, shock or chronic liver disease**, and neurocritical patients; ventilation alone is not a firm risk factor. Stop when the risk resolves, before discharge.
Evidence: REVISE 2024, **4,821** ventilated patients: pantoprazole cut bleeding **1.0% vs 3.5%** (NNT 40), with no change in 90-day mortality.
SUP-ICU 2018: less bleeding (2.5% vs 4.2%), same mortality. PEPTIC 2020, PPI vs H2 blocker: mortality 18.3% vs 17.5%, not significant.
Trade-off: a higher gastric pH was feared to cause VAP and C. difficile. In REVISE VAP was **23.2% vs 23.8%** and C. difficile **1.2% vs 0.7%**, both not significant.
What I do: low-dose PPI or H2 blocker (pantoprazole **40 mg**) only with risk factors, enteral or IV, reviewed daily. Catch: SUP-ICU's sickest (SAPS II >53) trended to more deaths.

questions.text: Investigations in acute pancreatitis. What are the limits of serum lipase?

steps.bridge: Diagnosis is 2 of 3: pain, enzymes over 3× normal, imaging. Next: which enzyme to send and where it misleads →
Lipase is more specific and stays up longer, but it is raised in renal failure and gut disease. Next: what tells severity instead →
Severity comes from BUN, haematocrit, CRP at 48 h and organ failure, not enzyme level. Next: which imaging, and when →
Ultrasound on day 1 for gallstones; CT is best after 72 h. Next: the bedside rule on when a CT is indicated →

spine: What it is: diagnosis needs **2 of 3**: typical pain, lipase or amylase **>3× ULN**, characteristic imaging. Pain plus enzymes is enough; no CT needed.
Lipase: preferred, more specific and stays up longer (late presenter). Limits: also raised in **renal failure**, bowel obstruction or ischaemia, perforation, cholecystitis, DKA.
Lipase level does not grade severity, and daily trending is useless. Amylase can be normal in alcoholic, hypertriglyceridaemic or late pancreatitis.
Other tests: ultrasound on admission for gallstones; triglycerides and calcium if no stones; BUN, haematocrit, CRP (**>150 mg/L at 48 h**) and ABG for severity.
When CT: not routinely. Contrast CT if the diagnosis is unclear or no improvement by **48–72 h** (ACG 2024); necrosis is reliably shown only at **5–7 days** (Atlanta).
Caution: an early CT under-calls necrosis and the contrast may worsen AKI. MRI if contrast is contraindicated or to see the duct; EUS or MRCP for CBD stones.

questions.text: Which is the best severity score for acute pancreatitis?

steps.bridge: Severe means organ failure lasting over 48 hours, not a score. Next: how organ failure is scored →
Modified Marshall ≥2 in lung, heart or kidney = organ failure; no score predicts it well. Next: the bedside 24-hour score →
BISAP: five items in the first 24 h, simple but modest. Next: the classic score that needs 48 hours →
Ranson needs 48 h, so it cannot triage at admission. Next: APACHE II and the single lab markers →
APACHE II above 8 and CRP above 150 at 48 h flag severe disease. Next: the CT score for local disease →
CT index grades necrosis and collections, best after 72 h. Next: the four-grade system that adds infected necrosis →

spine: Answer: **no single score is best**. ACG 2024: scores and imaging alone predict severe disease poorly; serial clinical reassessment over the first 48 h is what counts.
What defines severe (revised Atlanta 2012): **persistent organ failure >48 h**. Transient (<48 h) or local complications = moderately severe; none = mild.
Organ failure = modified Marshall **≥2** in respiratory (PaO2/FiO2 **≤300**), renal (creatinine **≥1.9 mg/dL**) or cardiovascular (SBP **<90** not fluid-responsive).
Scores: **BISAP** (5 items, 24 h, ≥3 high risk), **APACHE II >8** (any time), **Ranson** (11 items, needs 48 h), **CRP >150 mg/L at 48 h**, CT severity index after 72 h.
What I use: SIRS, BUN and haematocrit on admission and their trend; persistent SIRS or rising BUN means monitored bed. Organ failure despite fluids means ICU.
Caution: all scores have good negative but poor positive predictive value. The determinant-based system adds a **critical** grade (persistent OF + infected necrosis).

questions.text: How do you manage acute pancreatitis? What did WATERFALL show?

steps.bridge: The frame: moderate fluids, early feeding, no prophylaxis, step-up for necrosis. Next: which fluid, and why not aggressive →
Ringer's lactate, moderate and goal-directed; aggressive fluids risk ARDS and ACS. Next: the trial that settled the rate →
WATERFALL: aggressive fluids tripled overload with no benefit; stopped early. Next: analgesia and feeding →
Multimodal analgesia; feed by mouth early, NG if not, avoid PN. Next: the antibiotic question →
No prophylactic antibiotics, even in severe disease; treat proven infection. Next: when ERCP is indicated →
ERCP only for cholangitis or persisting obstruction. Next: test the traps across management →

spine: Frame: severity and monitoring, moderate fluids, analgesia, early feeding, no prophylactic antibiotics, ERCP for cholangitis, step-up for infected necrosis.
Fluids: **Ringer's lactate**, moderate. ACG 2024: no more than **1.5 mL/kg/h**, a 10 mL/kg bolus only if hypovolaemic; reassess within 6 h and for 24–48 h (BUN, haematocrit).
WATERFALL (de-Madaria, NEJM 2022, **249** pts): 20 mL/kg + 3 mL/kg/h vs 10 mL/kg if hypovolaemic + 1.5 mL/kg/h. Overload **20.5% vs 6.3%**; stopped for harm.
Primary outcome, moderately severe or severe pancreatitis: **22.1% vs 17.3%** (NS); deaths 3.3% vs 0.8% (NS). So aggressive fluid gave more overload and no benefit.
Feeding: oral low-fat diet within **24–48 h** as tolerated; NG tube if not eating by day 3; PN only if enteral fails. Multimodal analgesia; epidural is opioid-sparing.
Antibiotics: **no prophylaxis**, even in severe or necrotising disease. Treat cholangitis or proven infected necrosis (carbapenem). ERCP within 24 h only for cholangitis.

questions.text: Spotter: CT abdomen — chronic calcific pancreatitis / necrosis.

steps.bridge: Calcified ducts and atrophy mean chronic disease; a non-enhancing gland means necrosis. Next: name the collection by type and age →
Under 4 weeks: APFC or ANC; over 4 weeks: pseudocyst or WON. Next: how to score what the CT shows →
Necrosis carries more points than inflammation; 7–10 means about 17% mortality. Next: when to scan and rescan →

spine: Spot (chronic calcific): coarse **calcifications** within the gland and duct, a **dilated, beaded main duct** (chain of lakes), parenchymal atrophy, sometimes pseudocysts.
Cause: mostly alcohol. In India think **tropical calcific pancreatitis**: young, non-alcoholic, large dense duct stones; diabetes and cancer risk.
Spot (necrosis): on contrast CT, **non-enhancing pancreatic parenchyma**, with or without peripancreatic necrosis. Reliable only after the first week; gas means presumed infection.
Local complications (revised Atlanta): under **4 weeks**, APFC (fluid, no wall) or ANC (fluid and necrosis); over 4 weeks, **pseudocyst** (walled fluid) or **WON** (walled necrosis).
Others: infected necrosis, haemorrhage or pseudoaneurysm, splenic or portal vein thrombosis, gastric outlet obstruction, disconnected duct, colonic necrosis.
What I do: grade with the CT severity index; repeat CT on deterioration or before intervention. Intervene on collections only if infected or symptomatic, ideally after 4 weeks.

questions.text: How do you manage infected pancreatic necrosis?

steps.bridge: Early deaths are organ failure; late deaths, after 2 weeks, are infected necrosis. Next: how to diagnose and treat the infection →
Suspect from deterioration; gas on CT presumes infection; carbapenem; no routine FNA. Next: the ladder of intervention →
Delay to 3–4 weeks, then drain, then minimally invasive necrosectomy, open last. Next: the three trials behind it →
PANTER proved step-up, TENSION endoscopic equals surgical, POINTER that waiting is safe. Next: when to intervene without infection →

spine: What it is: infection of pancreatic or peripancreatic necrosis, usually after week 2; the main cause of late death. Suspect it in clinical deterioration with a collection.
Diagnose: **gas in the collection** on CECT, or clinical suspicion alone; routine FNA no longer advised. Start a carbapenem (necrosis-penetrating antibiotic).
Timing: antibiotics and support, **delay intervention to about 4 weeks** so it walls off (WON). Some never need drainage. Earlier only if deteriorating despite antibiotics.
Step-up: percutaneous or **endoscopic transgastric drainage**, then minimally invasive necrosectomy (VARD or endoscopic), open necrosectomy last.
Evidence: **PANTER** 2010 major complications or death **40% vs 69%**; 35% drainage only. **TENSION** 2018 endoscopic = surgical (43% vs 45%), fewer fistulas (5% vs 32%).
**POINTER** 2021: immediate vs postponed drainage, CCI **57 vs 58**, no benefit to early; postponed needed fewer interventions and **39%** never needed drainage.

questions.text: Abdominal compartment syndrome.

steps.bridge: Normal IAP is 5–7 mmHg; measure via the bladder every 4 h when at risk. Next: the exact technique →
Supine, zeroed at mid-axillary line, ≤25 mL saline, read at end-expiration. Next: the thresholds that define IAH and ACS →
IAH is 12 or more, graded I–IV; ACS is over 20 with new organ dysfunction. Next: the perfusion pressure that follows →
APP = MAP − IAP, aim 60 or more; the kidney sees IAP twice. Next: what the pressure does to each organ →
Venous return, lung compliance and urine fall; ICP rises; the gut feeds a vicious circle. Next: the medical levers →
Five levers: wall compliance, gut contents, collections, fluid balance, organ support. Next: when to open the abdomen →

spine: What it is: IAH = sustained or repeated IAP **≥12 mmHg** (grades I 12–15, II 16–20, III 21–25, IV >25). ACS = sustained IAP **>20 mmHg** with **new organ dysfunction**.
Measure (WSACS 2013): via the bladder, mmHg, **supine**, zeroed at the **mid-axillary line**, **≤25 mL** saline, read at **end-expiration** without abdominal muscle contraction.
Why it matters: venous return, lung compliance and renal perfusion fall; oliguria from about 15 mmHg. APP = **MAP − IAP**, aim **≥60**; renal gradient = MAP − 2 × IAP.
What I do: from IAP ≥12, sedation and analgesia ± NMB, NG and rectal decompression, drain ascites, avoid positive balance; measure at least every 4 h.
Overt ACS: **decompressive laparotomy** with temporary abdominal closure (WSACS 1D); primary ACS early, secondary after medical measures fail.
Caution: CVP and plateau read falsely high (half of IAP transmitted). ACS is not grade IV; WSACS made **no recommendation** on APP as a target.

questions.text: Nutrition in the ICU — when and how much?

steps.bridge: Stress makes its own glucose and breaks down muscle, so early full feeding overfeeds. Next: when to start the gut →
Enteral within 24–48 h, low dose, only once shock is controlled. Next: the current calorie and protein numbers →
Hypocaloric week 1, protein about 1.3 g/kg built up slowly, not high. Next: when the gut fails and PN must step in →
PN fills the gap: ESPEN by day 3–7, ASPEN not before day 7. Next: the danger of feeding a starved patient →
Insulin drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells. Next: who is at risk and how to start them →

spine: When: enteral within **24–48 h**, started low, once shock is controlled. PN only if the gut cannot be used or falls short: ESPEN by **day 3–7**, ASPEN after **day 7**.
Energy: hypocaloric first, **≤70%** of measured expenditure (ESPEN) or **12–25 kcal/kg/day** for 7–10 days (ASPEN 2022), then 80–100% after day 3. Early stress makes its own glucose.
Protein: build to about **1.3 g/kg/day** progressively (ESPEN); ASPEN 1.2–2.0. Not high early: EFFORT Protein no benefit and harm in AKI; PRECISe 2.0 vs 1.3 gave worse quality of life.
Refeeding: after starvation, insulin drives **phosphate**, potassium and magnesium into cells: arrhythmia, respiratory muscle weakness, heart failure, Wernicke's.
What I do: high risk (BMI <16, >15% weight loss, >10 days little intake, low K/PO4/Mg): **thiamine first**, **10 kcal/kg/day**, electrolytes daily, build over 4–7 days.
Caution: if phosphate falls below **0.65 mmol/L** or drops >0.16, ESPEN restricts energy for **48 h**, replaces it, then increases slowly.

questions.text: What are the calorie targets in early critical illness?

steps.bridge: Early on the body makes much of its own glucose, which feeding cannot switch off. Next: how we measure what he burns →
Indirect calorimetry is the gold standard; equations are rough guesses. Next: what the trials say about how much to give →
More calories early helped nobody; IC sets the target, not the speed. Next: the hidden calories that cause overfeeding →

spine: Why low early: in the first days stress hormones drive endogenous glucose production that feeding does not suppress, so full feeding on top **overfeeds**.
Targets: ESPEN 2023 **≤70%** of energy expenditure in the early phase, then **80–100%** of measured expenditure after day 3. ASPEN 2022: **12–25 kcal/kg/day** for the first 7–10 days.
Evidence: PermiT (40–60% vs 70–100%), TARGET (1.5 vs 1.0 kcal/mL, n≈4000) and EAT-ICU showed no gain from more calories; NUTRIREA-3 in shock favoured **less**.
Indirect calorimetry: measures VO2 and VCO2 (Weir); ESPEN says use it in ventilated patients. Without it, ventilator VCO2 beats equations, which mis-estimate both ways.
Caution: count propofol (**1.1 kcal/mL**), dextrose and citrate. Overfeeding brings hyperglycaemia, more CO2, harder weaning and fatty liver.

questions.text: What protein dose do you give in the ICU?

steps.bridge: Critical illness breaks down muscle fast, which is why protein was pushed. Next: how the dose is built across the stay →
Protein starts low and ramps to about 1.2–1.3 g/kg by week's end. Next: what happened when trials pushed it higher →
High protein gave no benefit and harmed those with AKI or high SOFA. Next: how protein changes with AKI and dialysis →

spine: What I give: build to about **1.3 g/kg/day** over the first days (ESPEN 2023). ASPEN keeps **1.2–2.0 g/kg/day**. Use pre-illness or adjusted weight in obesity and oedema.
EFFORT Protein (Lancet 2023, n=1329): **≥2.2 vs ≤1.2** g/kg prescribed (1.6 vs 0.9 delivered). No faster discharge alive; 60-day mortality **34.6 vs 32.1%**, not significant.
Who was harmed: baseline **AKI** (slower discharge, HR 0.5; 60-day mortality RR 1.4, mainly those not on RRT) and **SOFA ≥9**. Exploratory subgroups; urea rose.
PRECISe (Lancet 2024, n=935, blinded): **2.0 vs 1.3** g/kg enteral gave **worse** health-related quality of life to 180 days and more GI intolerance; mortality no different.
Caution: in AKI do not restrict protein to delay dialysis; on CRRT give **1.5–1.7 g/kg** to cover losses. Avoid early high doses in AKI not on RRT and in multi-organ failure.

questions.text: Should you feed a patient in shock?

steps.bridge: Uncontrolled shock and bowel ischaemia are absolute bars to enteral feeding. Next: what to do once shock is controlled →
Controlled shock on stable pressors: low-dose EN; full dose caused bowel ischaemia. Next: trophic versus full in ARDS →
EDEN: trophic for 6 days was as good as full, with less GI intolerance. Next: the shock trial that tested low versus standard →

spine: Yes, but low. In **uncontrolled** shock or rising lactate I hold enteral feed. Once MAP is stable on stable or falling vasopressors, I start low-dose EN within **48 h**.
Mechanism: in shock the splanchnic bed vasoconstricts; digestion raises gut oxygen demand, so full feeds can tip into non-occlusive bowel ischaemia.
Evidence: NUTRIREA-2 (n=2410): full-dose EN in shock gave more vomiting and bowel ischaemia (**2% vs <1%**) than PN, with no survival gain.
NUTRIREA-3 (n=3044): **6 vs 25 kcal/kg** and 0.2–0.4 vs 1.0–1.3 g/kg protein for 7 days: low was ready for discharge sooner (**8 vs 9 days**), same 90-day mortality, fewer GI complications.
Caution: stop and look if distension, high NG output, rising IAP or lactate. Advance toward target only after shock resolves, usually after day 3.

questions.text: Enteral versus parenteral nutrition - what is the evidence?

steps.bridge: Luminal feed keeps the villi, the barrier and gut immunity alive. Next: how the two routes compare head to head →
EN is cheaper and physiological; PN needs a line but avoids gut ischaemia. Next: what the big trials actually showed →
At matched dose the route barely matters; early PN on top of EN harms. Next: the rules for when PN is needed →

spine: Why EN first: it keeps the mucosa and gut immunity, is cheaper and needs no central line. But at matched calories the route matters far less than once thought.
CALORIES (n=2400): early PN vs EN for 5 days: 30-day mortality **33.1 vs 34.2%**, no more infections with PN; EN had more vomiting and hypoglycaemia.
NUTRIREA-2 (n=2410, shock): EN no better than PN for 28-day mortality (**37 vs 35%**) or infections, but more vomiting, diarrhoea and bowel ischaemia.
EPaNIC (n=4640): late PN (day 8) vs early PN: fewer ICU infections (**22.8 vs 26.2%**), faster ICU discharge, less cholestasis, shorter RRT; mortality the same.
When PN: EN contraindicated, PN within **3–7 days** (ESPEN; earlier and progressive if severely malnourished); EN falling short, supplemental PN after **day 7** (ASPEN), case by case.

questions.text: Do you measure gastric residual volume?

steps.bridge: Large GRV is one sign of gastric intolerance among several; routine checks are out. Next: the trials that removed them →
Not measuring GRV did not raise VAP and got more feed in. Next: how I treat true gastric intolerance →

spine: Not routinely. GRV was meant to warn of aspiration, but in trials checking it mainly stopped feeds and cut calories, without preventing pneumonia.
NUTRIREA-1 (JAMA 2013, n=449): no GRV monitoring was non-inferior for VAP (**16.7 vs 15.8%**); more vomiting, but more patients reached their calorie target.
REGANE (2010, n=329): a **500 mL** vs 200 mL limit delivered more feed in week 1 (**88 vs 84%**) with no more pneumonia, ventilation days or ICU stay.
What I do: no routine checks; I assess vomiting, distension and IAP. ESPEN: delay EN if GRV **>500 mL/6 h**; give IV **erythromycin** first, then post-pyloric if it persists.
Caution: rule out obstruction, ileus or ischaemia before pushing feeds or going post-pyloric.

questions.text: What is the NUTRIC score?

steps.bridge: Weight, BMI and skinfolds fail in oedematous ICU patients; muscle imaging and NUTRIC help. Next: the score itself →
Six items, mostly severity; high is 6–10, or 5–9 without IL-6. Next: what a high score should change, and the evidence →

spine: What it is: an ICU nutrition risk score (Heyland 2011): **age, APACHE II, SOFA, comorbidities, days in hospital before ICU, IL-6**. High risk **≥6**, or **≥5** on the modified score without IL-6.
Why: in observational data, more nutritional adequacy went with survival only in high scorers; each point raised the odds of 28-day death about **1.4-fold**.
How it changes feeding: high score, start EN early and reach target without delay; if EN is impossible and he is malnourished, early progressive PN rather than none.
Caution: RCTs did not confirm benefit; EFFORT Protein in high-risk patients showed no gain from more protein. ESPEN 2023: no ICU-validated score; treat all **>48 h** as at risk.
So I use it to prioritise attention, not to overfeed; hypocaloric start still applies.

questions.text: Hepatic complications of TPN.

steps.bridge: PN bypasses the gut; its liver risk is steatosis, plus line sepsis. Next: the full spectrum of PN liver injury and its causes →
Steatosis, cholestasis, sludge, then fibrosis; overfeeding, soybean lipid and sepsis drive it. Next: the hidden calories →
Propofol, dextrose and citrate add calories that overfeed. Next: telling PN cholestasis from sepsis or hypoxic liver →
Cholestasis has many ICU causes; exclude obstruction on ultrasound first. Next: the gallbladder catch in the septic PN patient →

spine: What it is: IFALD, formerly PNALD: liver injury from PN without another liver cause. **Steatosis**, **cholestasis**, gallbladder **sludge and stones**, late fibrosis.
Why: excess dextrose and energy make fat in the liver; soybean lipid (omega-6, phytosterols) impairs bile flow; sepsis adds; no enteral feed means biliary stasis.
Evidence: in EPaNIC, delaying PN to day 8 reduced cholestasis. Steatosis and cholestasis reverse; fibrosis is less reversible.
Prevent: avoid overfeeding, soybean lipid **<1 g/kg/day** or mixed fish-oil emulsions, cycle PN, keep some enteral feed, treat sepsis, avoid hepatotoxins.
Caution: exclude biliary obstruction and drugs with ultrasound and review; a septic PN patient with a tense gallbladder may have acalculous cholecystitis.

questions.text: What is the role of glutamine in burns?

steps.bridge: Burns are hypercatabolic: early EN, high protein, and no routine glutamine. Next: why it was given, and what the trial found →
RE-ENERGIZE showed no benefit; REDOXS showed harm in multi-organ failure. Next: the wider list of nutrients not to give →

spine: Why it was given: glutamine is conditionally essential in catabolism, a fuel for enterocytes and immune cells, and levels fall after burns. Small trials suggested fewer infections.
RE-ENERGIZE (NEJM 2022, n=1200): enteral **0.5 g/kg/day** in severe burns: time to discharge alive **40 vs 38 days**, 6-month mortality **17.2 vs 16.2%**: no benefit.
REDOXS (NEJM 2013, n=1223, multi-organ failure): IV plus enteral glutamine: 28-day mortality **32.4 vs 27.3%** (borderline), 6-month **43.7 vs 37.2%** (significant); worst with renal dysfunction.
Guidelines: ESPEN 2023 still lists 0.3–0.5 g/kg/day in burns >20% (Grade B), but says the largest RCT was negative and it needs revision; no glutamine in other ICU patients.
What I do: no routine glutamine. Focus on early EN, protein **1.5–2 g/kg/day**, and avoiding overfeeding.
